messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Animator
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Vignette:
Marisol had been twenty-five when the relationship that once felt ordinary and promising turned frightening and humiliating. She had met her boyfriend through friends and, for a while, thought she had found someone who understood her quiet, creative life as an animator. The abuse began in private, behind closed doors, in arguments that left her shaken and embarrassed, and then escalated into physical assaults that she now remembers in flashes of heat, force, and disbelief. What stays with her most is not one dramatic scene but the recurring certainty that when she tried to speak, protest, or leave a room, he would grab her, block her path, or strike out at her body so quickly that she had no time to think. She remembers the particular feel of being cornered in her own apartment, the sound of objects hitting the floor, and the way her body learned to brace before she even understood what was happening. At the time she told herself that she could calm him down, that if she chose her words more carefully or stayed quieter, it would stop.

After she left the relationship, those moments did not settle into the past in the way she expected. In the weeks that followed, Marisol found herself replaying the abuse in fragments, especially at night or when she was alone in her apartment. Certain moments returned with an almost immediate force: a raised voice in a neighboring apartment hallway, a hand reaching too quickly toward her shoulder, the sudden closing of a door, even the sight of an argument unfolding on a screen while she scrolled through videos after work. Each time, she would feel a rush of dread and tension in her body, as if something in the present had become unsafe without warning. She became wary in places that once felt routine. In the office, where she spends long hours at her drawing tablet with headphones on, she notices every sharp tone from coworkers and every unexpected step behind her chair. A colleague standing too close while looking at her monitor can make her stiffen before she has time to hide it. At home, she keeps the lights on longer than she used to and sits with her back against the wall when she can. Even simple tasks, like opening her front door after work or hearing footsteps in the stairwell, can leave her scanning the hallway and listening for what might come next.

Marisol has also come to see herself through the relationship in a harsher way than she ever did before. She says she should have known better, should not have ignored early warning signs, and should not have stayed once the behavior became physically threatening. She turns over the same self-accusations again and again, especially when she thinks about the nights she apologized to him or tried to smooth things over. In her mind, those moments now carry a painful moral weight: she feels that she acted in ways that did not fit the person she believed herself to be. As someone who grew up with strong ideas about loyalty, dignity, and never letting someone control her, she feels deeply unsettled by the fact that she sometimes complied or made herself smaller to get through the evening. She has told herself that staying quiet, not calling for help sooner, and trying to manage his moods meant she failed herself. More recently, she has begun to describe herself as permanently changed for the worse, as if something in her confidence and ease was damaged in a way that cannot be undone. Friends have noticed that she is more guarded and less spontaneous, but Marisol experiences it more privately, as a sense that the version of herself she used to know is gone.

These beliefs have made it hard for her to move through daily life with the same openness she once had. She avoids dating and keeps most interactions brief, saying she does not trust her own judgment anymore. She has also pulled back from some social plans because being around couples or hearing people talk casually about conflict can leave her feeling exposed and ashamed. At work she still performs well, but the effort of appearing calm takes energy, and she finds herself checking exits, measuring tone, and anticipating sharpness in ways that leave her exhausted by the end of the day. She came for help after a recent afternoon when a coworker jokingly grabbed her elbow to get her attention and she felt her whole body jolt before she could stop it. She went to the restroom afterward, locked the stall door, and realized she was shaking and angry at herself for still reacting so strongly. What frightened her most was the thought that this might be what her life is now: that she will always be on guard, that she will always blame herself, and that the part of her that used to feel steady and creative may never fully return. She is seeking help now because she wants relief from that constant vigilance and because, more than anything, she hopes to believe again that the abuse did not define who she is.
